newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn hails summit, urges NATO to respect Russia.
newsitem.headline: Bonn hails summit, urges NATO to respect Russia.

text.p: BONN, March 22 (March) - Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Russia's closest ally in the West, on Saturday hailed the summit between U.S. President Bill Clinton and President Boris Yeltsin as a success paving the way for new members to join NATO in July.

Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said in a statement Kohl welcomed agreements on nuclear disarmament and on including Russia in international economic institutions reached at the two-day Helsinki meeting.

"He stressed he was confident that in the coming months...mutual agreement will be reached on plans for NATO enlargement, the signing of a NATO-Russia charter and the start of NATO expansion," the statement said.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, who has played a significant role in diplomatic efforts to make NATO's plans more palatable to Russia, told the German newspaper Express the summit increased trust between the former Cold War foes.
But Kinkel warned alliance members an enlarged NATO would have to repect Russian security interests.
Kinkel also stressed that new NATO members in east Europe should not be treated as inferior.

"No one expected that, after the summit, Russia would say: 'Yes indeed, we are in favour of NATO expansion.' The important thing is that the ball is being played further ahead in the field," Kinkel told the paper.

Werner Hoyer, State Secretary in the Foreign Ministry, told German radio no more progress in talks on NATO expansion could possibly have been expected and that Yeltsin could not have made further concessions because of pressure at home.

Yeltsin agreed in Helsinki to sign a charter building a new relationship with NATO, despite Moscow's continued opposition to the eastward expansion of the alliance, and dropped a demand that the charter should be legally binding.
He also promised to minimise differences with the West over NATO enlargement, drawing charges from communist opponents in the Russian parliament Moscow had caved in.

Clinton pledged that east European countries would be able to join NATO as planned after the summit. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are the leading candidates to be invited to join after an alliance summit in Madrid in July.

Both Kinkel and Hoyer said NATO wanted a new security order in which Russia was included as a partner. "We must take Russia's legitimate security interests seriously and act accordingly," Kinkel said.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov visits Bonn where he meets Kinkel on Saturday March 29 to brief Germany on the results of the summit and discuss the planned charter between NATO and Russia and the admission of new members.
